claims.text: A managed Kubernetes service runs the cluster's control plane, managing its scale, availability, patches and upgrades; the team uses the API server address and credentials the provider gives and typically has no control-plane node to log in to.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Production environment > Production control plane ('Managed control plane' option)

claims.text: The provider keeps the managed control plane available and handles its patches and upgrades; this covers the kubeadm-era work of k8s/operators-and-cluster-lifecycle (etcd majority, etcd data, certificates, upgrade steps), summarised in the section 6 table.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Production environment (managed control plane); Operating etcd clusters; PKI certificates and requirements; Upgrading kubeadm clusters

claims.text: Node pools: worker nodes created from one template (machine size, Kubernetes version) that the provider keeps available; a broken node can be replaced from the template, so nodes are treated as replaceable and nothing set by hand is relied on.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Production environment ('Managed worker nodes' option); Node autoscaling (pre-configured node groups)

claims.text: Course working model, not a documented Kubernetes rule: providers publish which parts they run, and for a managed cluster the split usually leaves workloads, RBAC, NetworkPolicies, add-ons the team installs (Argo CD, cert-manager) and volume data on the team's side.
claims.source_hint: provider shared-responsibility documentation (not named); Kubernetes docs: Production environment

claims.text: Providers usually offer a set of minor versions and drop old ones on their own schedule (hedged, provider-dependent); Kubernetes rules still apply: skipping minor versions is unsupported, and manifests are checked for API versions the target stops serving.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Version Skew Policy; Release cycle / supported versions; Deprecated API Migration Guide; k8s.l3.cluster-upgrades

claims.text: LoadBalancer Services get external addresses and claims get network disks through the provider's cloud controllers and CSI driver (dynamic provisioning); the provider creates the disk, and nothing in the cluster backs up the data written on it.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Cloud Controller Manager; Service type LoadBalancer; Storage > CSI / Dynamic Volume Provisioning

claims.text: kubeadm.sh @ stage-3 lines 19-36: node() runs docker exec on donhang-control-plane (line 8, not shown); show() from scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh echoes then runs a command on the host; node ls / node kubeadm read the node, show kubectl asks the API server.
Whether a tier=control-plane Pod query finds anything on a managed cluster depends on how the provider runs the control plane (stated as provider-dependent, no default asserted).
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Static Pods (mirror Pods); Cloud Controller Manager

claims.text: self-run-components.md @ stage-3 lines 28-31: other self-run components incl., in the cluster, Argo CD, the Git server, the secret-decrypting controller and the incoming-traffic controller have the same recurring work; the team records them when they get an owner.

kubeadm.sh output @ stage-3: manifests etcd.yaml, kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml; four control-plane Pods on donhang-control-plane; certificate authorities ca, etcd-ca, front-proxy-ca; component certs 1 year, CAs 10 years.
With kubeadm the team can pass any control-plane flag through ClusterConfiguration extraArgs; a managed control plane usually exposes only the settings the provider offers (provider-dependent).
claims.source_hint: kubeadm docs: Customizing components with the kubeadm API (ClusterConfiguration extraArgs); provider docs (not named)

claims.text: A dynamically provisioned PersistentVolume inherits its StorageClass's reclaimPolicy, which defaults to Delete; deleting the bound PVC then deletes the volume and its underlying storage.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Persistent Volumes > Reclaiming > Delete; Storage Classes > Reclaim policy

claims.text: etcd (and an etcd snapshot) holds API objects, not data written to volumes.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Operating etcd clusters > Backing up an etcd cluster; k8s.l3.etcd-snapshots

claims.text: A new Kubernetes minor version can stop serving API versions; requests (e.g. an Argo CD sync) using them are then refused by the API server.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Deprecated API Migration Guide; Kubernetes Deprecation Policy

claims.text: Opinion: when a small team with no etcd expertise can rent machines, managed Kubernetes usually fits; when rules keep machines in-house, self-run kubeadm with the control-plane and cloud-part work budgeted.
Opinion: a needed API server setting or minor version the provider does not offer is a reason to change the need or self-run the control plane.
